title: The idea and properties of local search heuristics
text:
The idea of local search heuristics

A heuristic is a technique for approaching hard problems that does not give strong guarantees on the quality of the solution, but is efficient.

Local search heuristics are particular heuristic techniques for solving hard combinatorial optimisation problems that are based on the idea of searching the solution space.

Generally speaking, in a local search approach, we start with an initial feasible solution. In each iteration, we move from the current solution s to another "close" solution s' that is obtained from s by a small and quick modification. Each time, we evaluate the objective function while looking for the best solution.

Properties of local search

Positive properties:

- The approach is universal, meaning that it can be applied to any combinatorial problem.
- Algorithms based on local search are usually fast. More precisely, they have acceptably low, polynomial time complexity.

Negative properties:

- There is no guarantee of finding the global optimum.
- There is usually no guarantee of how much poorer the found solution is than the global optimum.

title: Binary relations and neighbourhoods
text:
Graph of a binary relation

Given a binary relation R ⊆ V × V on the set V, its corresponding directed graph G = (V, E) is defined as follows:

- The set of vertices is V.
- The set of edges E is exactly the set of all pairs v, v' ∈ V such that v is in relation R with v', meaning that (v, v') ∈ R.

Neighbourhood

For each current solution s, the set of solutions available in one iteration move from s to one of its neighbours is called the neighbourhood of s and is denoted N(s).

The neighbourhood is defined by a binary relation N ⊆ S × S on pairs of solutions, representing which pairs of solutions are neighbours. More precisely, s' is a neighbour of s if and only if (s, s') ∈ N.

Thus, the first step in approaching a problem with local search is to define the proper neighbourhood relation for that problem.

Example: Propose a neighbourhood relation for the Knapsack problem.

title: Properties of a good neighbourhood relation
text:
The desired properties of a well-defined neighbourhood relation are as follows:

- The relation should be connected. This is necessary to guarantee that the best solution is reachable from any starting solution.
- Any pair of neighbours should be similar to each other. This makes it possible to quickly modify one solution into a neighbour.
- For each solution, the number of neighbours should not be too large. This makes it possible to efficiently select a neighbour to move to.
- The diameter of the relation should be small. This provides an upper bound on the total number of iterations of the algorithm.

A well-designed neighbourhood relation has to satisfy all four properties.

Connectedness

A binary relation is connected if and only if its corresponding graph is connected. In other words, for any two vertices s and s', there is a path connecting them.

This property is necessary for the reachability of any solution from any other starting solution.

Example: In the Knapsack problem, a solution can be represented by a characteristic vector. How can the neighbourhood be defined to satisfy connectedness? Give one example of a neighbourhood relation on characteristic vectors that is not connected.

title: Similarity and size of a neighbourhood
text:
Similarity of neighbours

Any two neighbours should differ as little as possible. It should be computationally easy, in constant time if possible, to modify the representation of any solution s into any of its neighbours s'.

In addition, the objective function values of any two neighbours should differ very little. This describes the "flatness" of the solution-space landscape.

Example: Give one positive and one negative example of a neighbourhood relation for the Knapsack problem.

Small neighbourhood

The relation should be defined so that, for any solution s, the number of its neighbours is not too large. More precisely, the number of neighbours |N(s)| should be upper-bounded by a polynomial function of the task size.

This property guarantees that, in each iteration, the process of searching for the next neighbour is fast. More precisely, it has low, polynomial time complexity.

Example: Give one positive and one negative example of a neighbourhood relation for the Knapsack problem.

title: Diameter and implications of a neighbourhood relation
text:
Small diameter of the relation

The diameter of a relation is defined as the longest distance between any two elements in the corresponding graph of that relation.

The diameter of the neighbourhood relation should be upper-bounded by a polynomial function of the task size.

This property guarantees that the total number of iterations in the local search algorithm is acceptable. More precisely, its time complexity is bounded by a polynomial.

Example: For the Knapsack problem, give one positive and one negative example of a neighbourhood relation.

Implications of the properties

The four properties guarantee:

- The best solution can be reached because of connectedness.
- The local search algorithm has polynomial time complexity because of the other properties.

title: Random local search
text:
The simplest local search approach is to start with a random solution. In each iteration, the algorithm moves to a random neighbour and records the best solution found. This continues until the available time resources are exhausted.

For hard optimisation problems, the whole solution space is too large to be examined, so brute-force search is impossible.

There are many improvements to this basic random-search approach, including:

- Hill climbing.
- Simulated annealing.

title: Hill Climbing and its improvements
text:
Hill Climbing algorithm (HC)

Hill Climbing is a less "blind" approach than random search:

- Start with any random feasible solution.
- In each iteration, move from the current solution s to a neighbour s' that has the best objective function value among all neighbours of s.
- Continue until no neighbour of s is better than s.

This is a greedy approach because it evaluates only the neighbours of the current solution and selects the best one to move to.

Example: Propose a well-designed neighbourhood relation for the Knapsack problem and explain how HC behaves with this relation. What is its expected time complexity?

Improvements of HC

Possible improvements include:

- Restarting HC many times from different random starting positions.
- k-bundle search, which keeps a list of the top-k solutions at each iteration. This is different from restarting HC k times.

Despite these improvements, the HC approach always goes "up" in the solution-space landscape. This results in finding only the closest local optimum, not necessarily the global one.

In any variant of HC, the best solution seen is the one considered when the algorithm terminates.

title: Simulated Annealing and its high-level pseudocode
text:
Simulated Annealing (SA)

Simulated Annealing, unlike HC, makes it possible to occasionally "go down" in the solution-space landscape, but with a probability that decreases over time.

The name "simulated annealing" comes from an analogy to a process in metallurgy that consists of slowly cooling liquid metal to achieve a very regular and strong crystal structure.

High-level pseudocode of SA

current = initialRandomSolution()

while stopCondition:
    candidate = randomNeighbour(current)
    if f(candidate) is better than f(current):
        current = candidate
    else:
        current = candidate with probability P(current, candidate, f, temperature)
    lowerTemperature()

return bestSeenSolution

Here, f is the objective function.

The algorithm allows moving to a worse solution with a probability that decreases over time and with the degree of deterioration of the objective function.

title: Implementation and transition probability of Simulated Annealing
text:
Implementation of SA

The particular implementation depends on several decisions:

- A stop condition. Usually, this is that there has been no move for the last K iterations, where K is a parameter. This means that the algorithm is likely to be at a local optimum.
- A particular probability function.
- A particular cooling scheme that determines how the temperature is lowered.

Desired properties of the transition probability in SA

Assuming that the candidate is worse than the current solution, the transition probability function should satisfy the following properties:

- For a fixed current solution and candidate, the probability should decrease over time, represented by decreasing temperature.
- For a fixed temperature, the probability should decrease as the difference between the objective function values of the two solutions increases. It should be easier to move to a slightly worse solution than to a much worse one.

title: Transition probability and improvements of Simulated Annealing
text:
An example of a transition probability function in SA that satisfies the required properties is:

P(curr, cand, f, temp) = e^(-|f(curr) - f(cand)| / temp)

Since the probability decreases, the SA algorithm asymptotically tends towards the behaviour of HC as time elapses. However, it allows the algorithm to explore a wider range of the solution space at the beginning, when the temperature permits it.

Improvements of SA

There are many possible improvements to SA, including:

- Tabu search, which forbids returning to recently visited solutions.
- Tunnelling, which allows random jumps from time to time in order to "jump over" high and thin obstacles in the solution space.
